recommendations.source_detail: Stage 4 shows fleet GC at 6.45% of executor run-time (59,134,973 ms GC / 916,294,757 ms run-time). With 7 cores per executor sharing a 16 GB heap, each slot has ~2.3 GB. Peak execution memory per task in Stage 4 is uniformly ~785 MB, consuming ~34% of the per-slot share. Reducing to 5 cores raises per-slot heap to ~3.2 GB, giving each task ~40% more execution headroom and directly reducing GC frequency.
recommendations.rationale: Stage 4 GC is 6.45% — below the 12% health-gate threshold but elevated and fragile. The root cause is clear: 7 concurrent slots share a 16 GB heap (~2.3 GB/slot), and each task's peak execution memory (~785 MB) already consumes 34% of that share, leaving limited room before GC pressure escalates. Reducing spark.executor.cores from 7 to 5 increases per-slot heap to 16 GB / 5 = 3.2 GB without changing the container size or memory allocation — a pure division improvement. This is a single change within the executor-memory coupled cluster and must NOT be bundled with any memory or partition changes in the same run. The linear saving estimate from the tool (28.6% of vcore cost) is an overestimate because memory cost is unchanged; the real saving is near zero on cost (same container, fewer slots → fewer parallel tasks → potentially longer duration). The primary benefit is GC headroom and resilience, not cost reduction. Saving fraction is set near zero to reflect this: the change trades parallelism for stability, not cost. IMPORTANT: this recommendation must be applied AFTER the skew fix (ref=0) is observed to hold, since the skew in Stage 2 is the dominant pathology. These are in the same executor-memory coupled cluster — they must be serialized across visits. This recommendation is therefore sequenced as priority 2 (next visit after skew fix).
recommendations.explanation: With spark.executor.cores=7, the 16 GB executor heap is divided across 7 concurrent task slots, yielding ~2.3 GB of heap per slot. This run's executor peak managed execution memory reached 5.36 GB on-heap across the JVM (i.e. ~785 MB per slot at 7 slots), consuming ~34% of each slot's share and leaving a thin buffer before the GC must intervene — reflected in the measured gc_pressure of 5.74% and a raw JVM GC time of 71,114 seconds aggregated across executors. Reducing spark.executor.cores to 5 widens each slot's heap share to 16 GB / 5 = 3.2 GB (a 39% increase in per-slot headroom) without touching the container size, memory allocation, or any other parameter, directly reducing the frequency and duration of GC collection cycles.
recommendations.expected_impact: The primary benefit is GC resilience, not cost reduction: the container footprint is unchanged (same memory, fewer parallel slots), so the linear vCore saving estimate of 28.6% from the tool is an overestimate — real cost impact is near zero. The practical gain is that gc_pressure (currently 5.74%, with a 12% health-gate ceiling) gains meaningful headroom against data-volume growth or skew spikes, reducing the risk of a future GC-induced slowdown or OOM; any wall-clock improvement depends on whether GC pauses are currently on the critical path, which the 5.74% figure suggests is modest at present.
recommendations.risk_note: Fewer concurrent slots per executor means lower intra-executor parallelism; if the skew fix (priority 1) has not yet been applied and large tasks dominate Stage 2, reducing cores-per-executor could extend wall-clock duration — this change must be applied only after the skew fix is confirmed stable.

unactioned_insights.title: Stage 2 Skew: Max Task Duration 15× the Average
unactioned_insights.description: Stage 2 (the shuffle-write / parquet-read stage with 26,284 tasks) shows severe task duration skew: average task duration is ~11 s, p75 is 12 s, but the maximum is 167 s — a 15× ratio. The max-task executor run-time is 167,443 ms vs a median of ~9,754 ms. All disk spill (781 MB disk, 35.8 GB memory) is concentrated in this stage and in the tail tasks (max disk spill per task: 37.6 MB; max memory spill: 688 MB), confirming that a small number of hot partitions are exhausting per-slot execution memory while the rest of the fleet finishes quickly. The skew_ratio of 0.239 and skew_score of 156 corroborate this. This is a health-tier signal: the tail tasks inflate wall-clock duration and produce corrupted efficiency telemetry for the run.
unactioned_insights.reason: planner proposed 'spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes', which is not a recognised Spark/cluster config key — recommendation dropped

unactioned_insights.title: Dynamic Allocation + External Shuffle Service: shuffleTracking Explicitly Disabled
unactioned_insights.description: The job runs on YARN with dynamic allocation enabled (spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true) and an external shuffle service deployed (spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true). However, spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled is explicitly set to false. This is the correct and intentional configuration when an external shuffle service is present — the external service handles shuffle file retention so that executors can be released safely. The concern is that spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout is set to Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647 s ≈ 68 years), which means any executor that has cached data will never be released by dynamic allocation. The job shows no caching (cached_data_max_memory_size=0, cached_data_max_disk_size=0), so this setting is harmless today, but it is a latent misconfiguration: if caching is ever introduced, executors holding cached blocks will be pinned indefinitely, defeating dynamic allocation and causing resource leaks on the YARN cluster.

unactioned_insights.title: Speculation Enabled with 2,926 Speculative Task Launches on a Skewed Stage
unactioned_insights.description: spark.speculation=true is configured, and the run shows 2,926 speculative task retries (num_spark_tasks_retries=2,926 out of 37,377 total tasks — a 7.8% speculative launch rate). The retried_task_waste is 1.4% of total vcore-time (17,293 s wasted out of 1,238,915 s used). In Stage 2, the skew event shows the max task ran for 167 s while p75 was 12 s — speculation will aggressively re-launch these tail tasks, but because the slowness is caused by data skew (hot partitions spilling), the speculative copy faces the same hot partition and will also be slow or spill. This means speculation is consuming ~7.8% extra task slots and ~1.4% extra vcore-time without resolving the root cause (skew), and may be masking the true severity of the skew by occasionally winning the race. The retried_task_waste of 1.4% is below the health-gate threshold of 5%, so this is a performance/cost observation rather than a health issue.
unactioned_insights.reason: The speculation waste (retried_task_waste=1.4%, 2,926 speculative launches) is a downstream symptom of the Stage 2 data skew (ref=0). The insight's own suggested action explicitly states: fix the skew first, then re-evaluate speculation. Disabling spark.speculation before the skew is resolved would likely increase wall-clock duration. No config change is recommended this visit; the speculation behaviour should be re-assessed after the advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes change (ref=0) is applied and observed.

agent_insights.identifier: Stage 4 GC Pressure: Executor GC at ~6.5% of Run-Time with 7-Core Executors
agent_insights.title: Stage 4 GC Pressure: Executor GC at ~6.5% of Run-Time with 7-Core Executors
agent_insights.description: Stage 4 (the shuffle-read + Parquet write stage, 11,000 tasks) shows meaningful GC pressure: total executor JVM GC time is 59,134,973 ms against executor run-time of 916,294,757 ms, giving a fleet GC fraction of ~6.5%. Per-task GC distributions show p25=4,585 ms, median=5,947 ms, p75=6,876 ms, max=12,037 ms per task, against a median task duration of ~87,497 ms — so GC consumes roughly 6–7% of each task's time. This is below the 12% health-gate threshold but is elevated for a job running 7 concurrent slots per executor (spark.executor.cores=7) sharing a 16 GB heap. With 7 slots, each slot has only ~2.3 GB of heap to work with; the peak execution memory per task in Stage 4 is uniformly 822,083,584 B (~785 MB), meaning execution memory alone consumes ~34% of the per-slot share, leaving limited headroom before GC pressure rises further. This is a fragile state: a modest data volume increase will push GC past the health threshold.
agent_insights.evidence: Stage 4: internal.metrics.jvmGCTime=59,134,973 ms; internal.metrics.executorRunTime=916,294,757 ms → GC%=6.45%. taskMetricsDistributions jvmGcTime: p25=4,585, p50=5,947, p75=6,876, p100=12,037 ms. peakExecutionMemory per task: uniformly 822,083,584 B. spark.executor.memory=16g, spark.executor.cores=7 → ~2.3 GB heap per slot. executor_max_heap_memory_utilization=0.795 (79.5% of 16 GB heap used at peak). gc_pressure (run-level)=0.057.
agent_insights.suggested_action: Consider reducing spark.executor.cores from 7 to 5. This increases per-slot heap from ~2.3 GB to ~3.2 GB without changing the executor container size, directly reducing GC frequency in Stage 4. Verify GC% drops in the next run before making further adjustments.

triage_result.reasoning:
Applying the triage rules strictly against the measured run metrics:

**Tier 1 thresholds check:**
- retried_task_waste = 0.014 → below 0.05 threshold → Stage retries do NOT open health gate
- gc_pressure = 0.057 → below 0.20 (severe) and below 0.12 (executor fleet threshold) → GC does NOT open health gate
- spill_ratio = 0.000129 → far below 0.10 threshold → spill does NOT open health gate (has_spill=true is a presence flag only; with spill_ratio ≤ 0.10 it is a Tier 4 tuning observation)
- memory_headroom = 0.205 → well above 0.05 → no memory starvation
- skew_ratio = 0.239 → below 0.30 threshold for the conflict rule, and skew alone is not a Tier 1 pathology unless it crosses a measured threshold

**Insight-by-insight classification:**

**Insight 0 (Stage 2 Skew):** The insight narrative claims "health-tier signal" but the triage rules require measured thresholds to be crossed. skew_ratio = 0.239 (below 0.30 for the conflict rule), spill_ratio = 0.000129 (far below 0.10), retried_task_waste = 0.014 (below 0.05). None of the Tier 1 numeric thresholds are met. The skew is real and material (15× max/avg task duration, 781 MB disk spill concentrated in tail tasks), but the measured fleet-level spill_ratio is only 0.013% of I/O — a rounding error at fleet scale. This is a Tier 4 fine-tuning observation (shuffle partition / skew remediation), not a health pathology by the binding thresholds.

**Insight 1 (Stage 4 GC Pressure):** Fleet gc_pressure = 0.057, Stage 4 GC fraction ~6.5% — both below the 12% executor health-gate threshold and well below the 20% severe threshold. The insight itself acknowledges it is below the health-gate threshold. This is a Tier 4 fine-tuning observation (heap/core configuration fragility warning).

**Insight 2 (Dynamic Allocation + cachedExecutorIdleTimeout misconfiguration):** No caching is active (cached_data_max_memory_size=0), so this is a latent/future risk, not an active pathology. No Tier 1 threshold is crossed. This is a Tier 4 configuration tuning note.

**Insight 3 (Speculation + speculative task waste):** retried_task_waste = 0.014 < 0.05 threshold. The insight itself states this is below the health-gate threshold. 7.8% speculative launch rate and 1.4% vcore waste are performance/cost observations. Tier 4.

**Conflicts:**
- Insight 0 (skew) and any executor-reduction recommendation: skew_ratio = 0.239 is below 0.30 so the conflict rule (do not reduce executors when skew_ratio > 0.30 AND vcore_utilization > 0.60) does not technically fire. However vcore_utilization = 0.592 is also below 0.60, so the conflict rule is doubly not triggered.
- No memory reduction is recommended while has_spill=true and spill_ratio is known at 0.000129 (< 0.01), so the conflict rule "do not recommend memory reduction when has_spill=true AND spill_ratio unknown or ≥ 0.01" does not apply — spill_ratio is known and below 0.01.
- No active conflicts between the four insights themselves.

**Health gate:** No Tier 1 pathology is open. The health gate is closed (clean run). All four insights are efficiency/tuning observations and belong in Tier 4.

Total disk spill=781,517,898 B, memory spill=35,785,801,728 B. skew_ratio=0.239, skew_score=156. Skew event payload: avg=11 s, p75=12 s, max=167 s.
tier4.suggested_action: Investigate the hot partition(s) in Stage 2. With AQE enabled (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true), check whether spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled is active and whether the skewed partition is being split. If AQE skew-join handling is not firing (this is a SortAggregate, not a join), consider salting the grouping key or lowering spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes to produce smaller, more uniform partitions. Do NOT right-size executor memory or reduce resources until this skew is resolved — the spill and duration telemetry are driven by the tail tasks, not the steady-state workload.

tier4.identifier: Stage 4 GC Pressure: Executor GC at ~6.5% of Run-Time with 7-Core Executors
tier4.title: Stage 4 GC Pressure: Executor GC at ~6.5% of Run-Time with 7-Core Executors
tier4.description: Stage 4 (the shuffle-read + Parquet write stage, 11,000 tasks) shows meaningful GC pressure: total executor JVM GC time is 59,134,973 ms against executor run-time of 916,294,757 ms, giving a fleet GC fraction of ~6.5%. Per-task GC distributions show p25=4,585 ms, median=5,947 ms, p75=6,876 ms, max=12,037 ms per task, against a median task duration of ~87,497 ms — so GC consumes roughly 6–7% of each task's time. This is below the 12% health-gate threshold but is elevated for a job running 7 concurrent slots per executor (spark.executor.cores=7) sharing a 16 GB heap. With 7 slots, each slot has only ~2.3 GB of heap to work with; the peak execution memory per task in Stage 4 is uniformly 822,083,584 B (~785 MB), meaning execution memory alone consumes ~34% of the per-slot share, leaving limited headroom before GC pressure rises further. This is a fragile state: a modest data volume increase will push GC past the health threshold.
tier4.evidence: Stage 4: internal.metrics.jvmGCTime=59,134,973 ms; internal.metrics.executorRunTime=916,294,757 ms → GC%=6.45%. taskMetricsDistributions jvmGcTime: p25=4,585, p50=5,947, p75=6,876, p100=12,037 ms. peakExecutionMemory per task: uniformly 822,083,584 B. spark.executor.memory=16g, spark.executor.cores=7 → ~2.3 GB heap per slot. executor_max_heap_memory_utilization=0.795 (79.5% of 16 GB heap used at peak). gc_pressure (run-level)=0.057.
tier4.suggested_action: Consider reducing spark.executor.cores from 7 to 5. This increases per-slot heap from ~2.3 GB to ~3.2 GB without changing the executor container size, directly reducing GC frequency in Stage 4. This is a single change within the executor-memory coupled cluster. Do not bundle with any memory or partition changes in the same run. Verify GC% drops in the next run before making further adjustments.

tier4.identifier: Dynamic Allocation + External Shuffle Service: shuffleTracking Explicitly Disabled
tier4.title: Dynamic Allocation + External Shuffle Service: shuffleTracking Explicitly Disabled
tier4.description: The job runs on YARN with dynamic allocation enabled (spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true) and an external shuffle service deployed (spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true). However, spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled is explicitly set to false. This is the correct and intentional configuration when an external shuffle service is present — the external service handles shuffle file retention so that executors can be released safely. The concern is that spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout is set to Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647 s ≈ 68 years), which means any executor that has cached data will never be released by dynamic allocation. The job shows no caching (cached_data_max_memory_size=0, cached_data_max_disk_size=0), so this setting is harmless today, but it is a latent misconfiguration: if caching is ever introduced, executors holding cached blocks will be pinned indefinitely, defeating dynamic allocation and causing resource leaks on the YARN cluster.
tier4.evidence: spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout=2147483647 (Integer.MAX_VALUE). spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true. spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true. spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled=false. cached_data_max_memory_size=0 B, cached_data_max_disk_size=0 B (from metrics). num_executors peaked at 1,764 during the run.
tier4.suggested_action: Set spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout to a reasonable value (e.g. 3600s or 1800s). This has no effect on the current job (no caching in use) but prevents a future resource leak if caching is added. This is a zero-risk change for the current workload.

tier4.identifier: Speculation Enabled with 2,926 Speculative Task Launches on a Skewed Stage
tier4.title: Speculation Enabled with 2,926 Speculative Task Launches on a Skewed Stage
tier4.description: spark.speculation=true is configured, and the run shows 2,926 speculative task retries (num_spark_tasks_retries=2,926 out of 37,377 total tasks — a 7.8% speculative launch rate). The retried_task_waste is 1.4% of total vcore-time (17,293 s wasted out of 1,238,915 s used). In Stage 2, the skew event shows the max task ran for 167 s while p75 was 12 s — speculation will aggressively re-launch these tail tasks, but because the slowness is caused by data skew (hot partitions spilling), the speculative copy faces the same hot partition and will also be slow or spill. This means speculation is consuming ~7.8% extra task slots and ~1.4% extra vcore-time without resolving the root cause (skew), and may be masking the true severity of the skew by occasionally winning the race. The retried_task_waste of 1.4% is below the health-gate threshold of 5%, so this is a performance/cost observation rather than a health issue.
tier4.evidence: spark.speculation=true. num_spark_tasks_retries=2,926; num_spark_tasks=37,377 → 7.8% speculative rate. executors_used_vcore_time_of_retried_tasks=17,293,096 ms; executors_used_vcore_time=1,238,915,276 ms → retried_task_waste=1.4%. Stage 2 skew: max task=167 s, p75=12 s. SparkListenerSpeculativeTaskSubmitted fired 3,246 times (from events stats payload).
tier4.suggested_action: Fix the Stage 2 data skew first (see skew insight). Once skew is resolved, re-evaluate whether speculation is still needed. If the skew fix eliminates the tail tasks, the speculative launch rate and associated vcore waste should drop substantially. Disabling speculation before fixing skew would likely increase wall-clock duration.
